utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr President and your Honours. We have another protected witness, I believe this is Witness X, if I am not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This is in all likelihood, Mr President, our last witness with regard to the Busovaca area. With regard to the specific events he will talk about, he will briefly talk about the build up of pressure and the growing number of HVO soldiers in the Busovaca area subsequent to May 1992, how the Croats put pressure on other Croats to join the HVO. He will also talk about what exactly happened in January when the conflict broke out, and the individuals in his village were forced, rounded up and taken to Kaonik camp. He was not taken simply because he was watching from the woods, he was lucky enough not to be home at the time. He will then talk about the conflict to some degree, he will talk about the burning of houses in and around that timeframe in his little village. He will then move ahead to talk about what happened after these Muslims in his village -- the houses were vacated, how members of the HVO who were from the town of Busovaca moved into many of these houses and then thereafter some houses were taken over by some refugees or Croats from other areas such as Kacuni. He then will move ahead and will talk about the events that took place in April -- we will not repeat, of course, your Honour what your Honours have heard already, but he will talk about the specific killings that took place in his area where his neighbours were killed, how his house was burnt, how his neighbour's house was burnt, individuals were injured, how he, and this is directed, Judge Riad, to something you asked this morning, how he specifically informed the HVO whether or not this individual Zoran had been arrested. They informed him that he had been arrested when, of course, when he was in hiding he saw Zoran driving around the street and Zoran had never been arrested and has never been prosecuted, albeit a member of the HVO and the information had been brought to the HVO authorities. Given that situation, he decided to vacate and leave Busovaca in the first week of May 1993. Similar to much of what has been set out by my colleague Mr Harmon this morning, the evidence you will hear, your Honours, will be directed in large part towards, of course, the persecution count, it will be directed towards count 5 and 10, the unlawful killings, and that will be the focal point of those particular charges at this time. He will have some information, of course, about the inhumane treatment of people, but he was not taken away to dig trenches. However, he will discuss the digging of trenches not only in January but also in April. As I said at the outset, Mr President and your Honours, he was in the woods when he saw his neighbours being led away and he was not led away. However, he will tell us that in April, the HVO ordered a Muslim to take a list of Muslims, to go throughout the area of Busovaca and round up Muslims on a daily or nightly basis to take them out to dig trenches, and this was as late as April 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, you have accepted to come here as a witness in the case against General Blaskic, and you have been asked by the Office of the Prosecutor. We expect from you now a statement about what you saw in Busovaca and what happened after May 1992 and also after April 1993. Please be concise and speak about the events of which the Prosecution tries to bring our attention to. Please, Prosecutor, you can ask some preliminary questions and after that, leave the witness to give their statement. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr President. Good afternoon, Witness X.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Witness X, how old are you, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am 51 years old.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Witness X, are you a Bosnian Muslim?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Until May 1993, did you live around the town of Busovaca, or in a suburb of Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Witness X, if you could, could you tell us a little bit about your particular mahala, your particular suburb, and then tell us what happened from May 1992 through the events in May to January to April 1993, until your departure in May 1993. Could you do that for us, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. First of all I would like to say something about the communal life between the Croats and Muslims in Busovaca before the war. Those relations were real, we respected each other, there were never any problems. However, in 1990 and 1991, I noticed that the Croats and the Muslims started pulling apart and the Muslims -- we the Muslims did not know what was going on, that is we were not aware that there could be anything between these two communities. In 1991 the elections were held and everything was all right. However, after the elections we noticed that the Croats started pulling away from the Muslims, they were not socialising the way they used to before the war, so one could notice that something was not right. Personally, I could not decipher what it was. I had no idea of any conflict being possible, so I went about my regular life. However, in early 1992, when the JNA attacked Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Croats and Muslims started separating even more. The Croats started wearing the HVO uniforms with the HVO insignia, while the Muslims did not have such uniforms. Nobody was wearing such uniforms, and I thought I would ask some of the Croats that I knew better what this meant, and they said that we had to fight the JNA, the Serbs, because Bosnia had been attacked. So that is how I understood it and accepted it, until we noticed that something else was going on. I was about 1.5 kilometres from the centre of Busovaca, where more Muslims than Croats lived, but there was -- nobody abused anyone because one group was larger than the other, that is until 1992. In early May, there was a conflict at the Kaonik barracks concerning some weapons, because this used to be a JNA barracks, so there was a conflict there. However, an agreement was reached, even though later the HVO took over the control of the local government in the local police station, so that we, the Muslims, could see that this was no longer defence against the JNA but that it was becoming critical for the Muslims to stay in the area. As days and months went by, more and more we noticed that the Croats had more uniforms, more weapons, the HVO insignia, and the pressure and intimidation became more frequent. Personally I noticed that something was amiss, that those of us -- we could be the victims here. I did not understand that I would need to leave my house, the house that I had built with my own money. In early 1993, in January, starting in January, one could see that some Muslims were starting to leave, which I did not understand because I could not believe that I would have to leave Busovaca. We always lived there together, both Croats and Muslims, so that I stayed at my home. On one occasion, I asked a Serb why he was leaving, why they were leaving, because in 1992, Serbs were leaving Busovaca and they had a collection centre in a village called Podjele, from Novi Travnik, from Zenica, from Travnik and they were going towards Kobiljaca, which is where the border was where the Serb Army was positioned. The price was 1,000 to 2,000 German marks, depending on what they were taking with them, a car or a tractor. If they were taking more belongings along, they would be obliged to pay more money. I asked the Serb why they were leaving and he said, "that is because they are chasing us away right now, but your turn will come too". So I understood that as a joke, I thought they were going of their own free will, that nobody was expelling them, but on 23rd January 1993 -- 24th January 1993, I came back from Zenica to Busovaca, I had been in Zenica and I asked a friend of mine, I encountered him in town and I asked him what was going on and he made a gesture with his hands as if I needed to leave, that there would be some kind of trouble. So I came home, it was already late to leave there at that time, even though some Muslims had left on the previous Friday, which was the 22nd, the 21st, two or three days before the conflict itself. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before the conflict, some Muslim refugees from Jajce came. There were a lot of Muslim weekend houses and they would move into these homes with the agreement of the owners of these homes, so there were these refugees from Jajce there. However, the conflict broke out on the 25th, that is over there in Kacuni. It started because an HVO vehicle, which was a makeshift armoured vehicle, they launched an attack. When you go down the road towards Busovaca, the Kiseljak-Busovaca road was always open, nobody was open and when they were going towards this barracks, our people stopped them. There was a silo there where wheat was kept, a very large silo, 10,000 tonne, and I guessed they were trying to take control of that, and maybe the barracks too. So some fire was exchanged. Two HVO soldiers died, and then the conflict broke out. I could hear that down in Busovaca, there was shooting in the hills, I could hear detonations from explosions and then I realised that the conflict had started and that it was too late to go anywhere. On the 26th in the morning, the HVO started a massive house search in town, in Busovaca and around in the surrounding areas where they knew that the Muslims lived. They were searching for weapons, for radios, transmitters, anything that could be used in the war. However, I doubt very much that they found any radio transmitters because none of us could have bought one, nor did we need them. And then on the right-hand side from the road near Busovaca, there were about 20 Muslims who had hunting rifles of two kinds, and you could observe from there what was going on in Busovaca, because that was about 100 to 200 metres from Busovaca in a straight line, so you could observe very well what was going on down in Busovaca. So they offered resistance, both those who did find some weapons and those who did not, and those who were going in the direction of Kaonik, this collection centre. I was not there so I cannot tell you exactly what was down there in Kaonik. So this exchange of fire went on for a couple of hours and then the Muslims surrendered and surrendered the weapons that they had and then they were taken to Kaonik, all of them. I was about 1,500 metres from Busovaca in the opposite direction, so I could not see all this in detail, because I was not present at the scene. The next week, some time mid-week, so on 27th, 28th or 29th January, there were more house searches because we were maybe up to ten permanent residents who had stayed in the mahala, in this neighbourhood, and there were the refugees from Jajce. However, the refugees from Jajce were driven out of their homes, out of the property of the people who were from other areas, from Sarajevo and Zenica, and they were moving Croats in. I knew a few of them, so some of them were moving in, or maybe they would move in for two or three days, then they would take some belongings from there that they wanted and needed and then they would move into another house. I saw some of these things myself. After a few days, the military police arrived in my neighbourhood and they started arresting the Muslims who had remained, those ten who had stayed there and the refugees from Jajce. Those who were of military age they were taking to Kaonik and women whereby then later driven away through the auspices of

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So after they had been arrested -- again, I should stress that I was not at home at that time, I was in one of the weekend homes at that time, but I could observe from there because it was not a great distance. When I saw they were being arrested, I left this weekend house. I came to the edge of the wood. There was a refugee from Jajce there, so I sort of hugged the edge of the wood so they would not see me. Nobody said that I was there where I was, so that I had stayed in my neighbourhood. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 15 (redacted) Later there were more house searches by people who came. The police, they looked for radio transmitter and weapons and I told them that all my neighbours, Croats, know that I never engaged in such things and that I was not even a hunter, I did not even have a hunting rifle. I have no weapons, let alone a radio transmitter. I did not expect any conflict with my neighbours. On one occasion, there was a refugee, a Croat from Kacuni who lived in a house of a neighbour of mine who had fled earlier, so there was a house search and we went to the basement. He asked me, "why are you following me?"; I said, "if there is nobody around, sometimes some people would throw in a rifle or some piece of weapon and claim that there is weapons there that were not reported, so that is what I was afraid of". I told him that I would follow him as he was searching so that I would be sure that no weapons would be discovered. He was a bit angry and then gave up the search. So on 23rd January, they came again to the (redacted) house and they came over to my house. Then again they searched the houses and they told us that we were not to leave the premises and our backyards, due to the safety concerns. I had no reason to go anywhere, to go down to the town because I had food supplies, so I did not have any need to go, to buy anything like that. On 26th January --

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Witness X. You just said 23rd January and 26th January.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I got a bit confused. On 23rd January, that is what I said, but what I meant was 23rd April. It was three days before those two men came. I am sorry, because I made a mistake here, because I wanted to link that up to the fact that on 23rd April those people came, those people who did to us what they did. It was not them who came, but some other people who told us not to go out and to remain there for our own safety. I am sorry, I just was confused. On the 26th, in fact on the 14th April, the second conflict broke out between the HVO and the Territorial Defence, so there was shooting going on everywhere, and nobody knew where to go and what to do and where we were, but we stayed on in our houses, nobody went out and nobody came and nobody mistreated us or put pressure on us or threatened us. We were relatively safe up until 26th April at 10.00 pm. I was at home with my family and so around 2200 hours, somebody knocked at the door. I said to my wife, "shall I answer?", and she said, "no, do not answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: asked, "who is it?", and they said, "open the door, it is the police. Where is (redacted)?". Then very quickly, because the door was locked, I agreed with my wife that I should jump out of the house through the window, because it was on the ground floor and that they should stay at home, because I understood as they were asking of me that something was wrong. I went out, I jumped out of the window on the side of the house which is opposite to the house entrance and so from that side, I went around the house further away and went to a neighbour's house, a Croat, which is to the right-hand side of my house when you go towards the road, there was an elderly Croat who lived there, aged 60 or 61, he was on his own at home. In fact it was his son's house and he came there just for a weekend, but stayed on because of the conflict. His son worked somewhere abroad, so that person used to come on several occasions, even before the war in that particular house. I asked him for help and I said, "some kind of a police came, they are probably Croats. Could you please help me and could you explain to them", and so on, and he answered, "I cannot help you I must not dare", something like that. I was rather frightened. So I went towards my house and arrived to the window of my kitchen. In the kitchen, the lights were on and in the dining room we could only hear the television. I could see at the dining table a person whom I could see very clearly and a bit further away there was somebody else who I could not see. Maybe the easiest thing would be to show it on a piece of paper actually. So the kitchen window was open because my son also wanted to jump out of the window, but he did not manage to do so because they came in before he did that, so the window was just slightly open and there was the curtain, so I could hear them well, I could hear what they were saying. They asked when they came in about me and my wife said that I went out in the neighbourhood that evening and that I still had not come back. What I would like to stress: when I came back from seeing that Croat whom I asked for help, I could see on my way back that part of the house was already on fire and in one of the rooms, one of the blankets was caught up in the fire and the flames were going out of the window. Then I suppose that they set the house on fire and they insisted very forcefully on where I was. My wife, as I said, had told them that I had gone out somewhere in the neighbourhood, they were insisting and insisting and they were shooting in the -- they fired in the ceiling and I saw the arms of the person whom I could not otherwise see, he took a knife and put it under my wife's throat, so that she would tell him where I was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Would you maybe like to have a little rest?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I would prefer to end my story first and then maybe after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As my family did not say where I was, because in fact they did not know where I was, they knew I was outside but not even them, they did not know that I was just standing by the window, so they insisted for some 15 minutes maybe, those people, and then they were told not to go out of the house, that they were going to kill them. They went to seek me. But when I saw them going out, they said they would be coming back. I went slightly more further away, which you can see it in the picture, there is another building there, so they went out in the direction of the road. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (redacted), I went into the house, I took my family and directed them towards the woods that were at the end of our neighbourhood. It was just near a Croat house and I was sure that they were not going to look for them there, because it was also during the night. I stayed in front of the house, I took a hose and tried to quench the fire, but that was too late and then I went to the other side of the house, which was not on fire, and took some belongings out and then I realised there was no point in taking anything out because the smoke was very dense. I started to suffocate and the fire caught in the other room as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understood from that that she was also told that nobody should go anywhere and that she simply said, "yes, that is okay". Then I decided that depending on where they would go, I would either go towards the road and in case they went to the other side, that I would remain where I was. So they went to the other side and I remained where I was, but when they arrived to the entrance gate of my house, and this house is some 25 metres away from the road, they went up the stairs and I went down near the other building, and I stayed there. They came somewhere halfway towards the house, they were on the steps, and they were shooting incendiary bullets and then they came back and swore and one said to the other that they were not quite satisfied, the job was not done properly, and they let some people go. Then they went out of my house towards the left where the house of Zoran Marinic was and of Mirko. I thought that would be the end, that there would not be any kind of torture any more. My house was on fire but nobody was hurt and I was resigned to that, so I went to try and find my family, I realised I could not put the fire down in my house. I went out on the street and towards where I said my family to go and find shelter. When I was going across the street and in the meadow, some 20 or 30 metres, when I was on the road, I could see Zoran's car going on the house, and I thought at first that it was the police, that somebody has called the police, but I simply jumped on the floor, so that they could not see me with the lights, and I could see a car, a blue car owned by Zoran Marinic. He had moved in a weekend house and I could see him every day. That weekend house used to belong to the person from Zenica, if need be I can even say that owner's name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: ` 24 to 20 minutes to find my family, it was all during the night, I called for them, they did not dare call back, they were afraid, but we managed to communicate and we went, all of us, on the meadow near the house of that Croat. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (redacted). In the meantime the police had arrived. The Croat who told me he could not help, he went to the police station and the fire men came and the police -- the fire men tried to put down the fire of my house. (redacted) As the house was on fire, everything was lit up and one could see for some 50 or 80 metres what was going on. I could see they were taking something out of the house but I could not see what. I woke up a Croatian neighbour who was also in the police and I had confidence in him. I asked him to go down there and see what was going on. He went down there, he was away for some 10 or 15 minutes and when he came back, he told me that everybody was killed (redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: the (redacted) was still conscious and he told the police straight away who committed all that. I did not know where to go, it was all during the night and what to do, but my neighbour's mother went out of the house and she said that we could stay in their house, that probably nobody was going to look for us at that moment, so that was what we did, we stayed there until the morning. I asked my wife to go to fetch help from UNPROFOR, so that they would take us out of the area. She went there very early in the morning and I went in front of my house, (redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (redacted). I went towards the neighbour's house, that Croat in whose house I spent the night, and the police came and wanted to have a statement from us, knowing who did that -- and wanted to know who did it. I told him, "you probably know much better than I do who did it". They told me, "you have to come with us to the police station and we are going to take a statement from you". I went down to the police station, gave the statement and just as I told you here, I told them what had happened regarding the killings and the burning down of houses. In the meantime, my wife arrived from UNPROFOR, and I asked her whether we could go and she said that the police had to give a permit to UNPROFOR because otherwise UNPROFOR would not want to take us out of the area. I said that we wanted to leave at any cost, because we were afraid, and they told us, "you are not going to go anywhere; anyway, go out of here and then we will see". My wife and I went out of that office for some ten minutes and after that time, they called me and told me that we could not go anyway from Busovaca, and they asked me whether there was a weekend house that was vacant in my neighbourhood in Busovaca where we could live. I said, "I do not want to stay here any more because if you came to try and kill me in my house, I am not going to stay in somebody else's house". They asked me whether I had any relatives there, and I said, "no, I have no relatives there", because I wanted to go out of the area. Then they said, "there is somebody called Redzo Delijic at Busenji, there are more Croats in that village". In that village there were only two Muslim houses and out of two Muslim houses, one Muslim family stayed and the other one left. The road that we took, there was a relative of mine who lived there. He also had left during the conflict. He drove away a wounded woman. They were also shooting into his house, they were five or six people in his house at that time and as there was shooting. One woman was injured, so he drove her away to Zenica. His wife remained on her own there. So I said to them that that was the house where I had to go because they did not know that person, so they thought that it was the house and I went out. I saw my relative's wife in front of the house and they went back. I thought to myself they were probably going to look for me again, and within an hour, we went back to town. We came to a street where there were more Muslims that had remained, there were mostly Muslims there. I was hiding in a house of a woman. That house was very near the street and I could see who was going there in the street. I spent seven days there. I saw Zoran and somebody else with him. They were looking for me. I was informed that they were looking for me. On many occasions, I would see him go down the street, two or three times per day. But there is something I would like to stress. I arrived there after that tragedy, around 3rd or 4th May. There was a Muslim who came to the house of the woman where I was hiding and he showed a list of us Muslims that had remained. I asked him what that was. He answered that that was the list of the Muslims who remained because of their work, and they had to go and dig trenches on the front-line. I asked him whether they were calling everybody to do that and he said, "no, according to the needs. Sometimes they need 10 or 15 people. Some people would work for 24 hours, others for 10, 15 hours", so those people would go regularly to dig trenches on the frontline. I was not there, but I suppose that they were digging trenches. I asked him why he had to do that. He said, "I had to do that because I was the one who knows -- I am the one who knows very well who stayed and so on and they give me how many people I have to bring and where". So he would bring those people to the HVO and then the HVO would do with those people what they wanted to, and that was like that every day. I told him, because my name was not on the list, "please do not mention my name because in case I go to the front-line, they will know that I am here and that will be my end". He said, "no, no, I will not ask for you -- in case they do not ask for you". I said, "neighbour, they do not know that I am here and where I am". He told me not to fear anything. On 4th May 1993, my cousin's wife arrived and she told me that Zoran with two others were looking for me in the Busenji village where I was supposed to be. They told her they were going to kill everybody and put everything on fire in order to find me, they were asking where I was. She came to tell us that. I told my wife, she was less known, she did not meet those people as I did. I asked her to go to the police station and try and in one way or the other get the permit for us to leave. She went to the police and asked for that permit and they told her, "it will be done within two or three days. There will be an exchange made then and so everybody who wants can go", but that she could not get the permit at that moment. What I did not say in the statement, they asked her where we were hiding for a week, and she answered, "there where you sent us to go, but we are not in the house, we are in the woods", because there were some woods there about 150 metres from there and she said we were simply there day and night. The commander told her, "go where you came from, we are going to send a police patrol to you right away". My wife came to me and told me that, and I told her, "we have to leave in any case", because I knew, in case they found us in that house where there was somebody else there, a husband and wife who had been expelled from their house three days earlier and there was also the family of that woman there. I told my wife, "it really would not be right that somebody else gets killed because of me", so we should go, we should go through the town. There used to be a railroad there to Zenica, and there only remained a path now, and there was some fields there, so I suggested we should go two by two, so that nobody would notice that we were refugees, in case we were in a group. There was another woman there who came from Gavrine Kuce, that is a village towards Zenica, and during the conflict she happened to be at her sister's house. She has a son who is ten years old or so and they came with us. I sent her and her son in front of us and we remained some 100 or 150 metres behind them. I was going with my younger daughter and my older daughter and my wife and that woman were going behind us, so we went out of the house with a distance of some 150 metres. So we went out of the town, we took that rail track and we came to a company and a brick manufacturing factory and then we went to Kaonik where there is a junction, Travnik-Zenica-Busovaca, and then we also continued to go separately and then we went to our control point, towards Gavrine Kuce and then we went to Zenica. I would like to stress that the Muslims who remained in Busovaca after we left in 1993, they were exchanged, because quite a few soldiers came from Zenica to Busovaca. There was an exchange. For example, if I wanted to leave Busovaca, I had to ensure that a family from an HVO soldier from Zenica would come to Busovaca, so I would be allowed to leave Busovaca to go to Zenica. That is how things were in 1993, I was in Kacuni and I was an eyewitness when one of our soldiers had his wife and daughter that remain, and also there was at another place at Kacuni there was an HVO soldier whose mother had remained there so they decided to make an exchange between Kacuni and Busovaca. That exchange went well. I think that maybe there were some three Muslims that stayed on. One of them was severely disabled and there were two that did not want to leave, they were father and son, and there were also some 20 elderly women all in all who remained there during the whole period of war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Witness X. In your statement, you have covered all the events that the Prosecutor wanted you to talk about. Mr Kehoe, would you like to point out anything else, some additional questions, or would you prefer to make a short break? Do you have many questions to ask, Mr Kehoe?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I have a few matters to cover just to clarify a few things and two exhibits, Mr President. Whether or not there is a break, I leave that up to your Honours and the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: How do you feel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: In that case, we will make the break after the Prosecution has finished. Mr Kehoe, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr President. Witness X, I am going to ask you now a few questions based on the narrative that you just gave the court. At the outset, I would like to show you a series of photographs, if we could, Mr Dubuisson, the photograph album.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 241.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: We do not need to put this on the ELMO. I am not going to go through these photographs in series, but Witness X, the series of photographs that I have before you is a series of photographs of your house and the surrounding areas prior to the conflict, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: These are photographs that were taken in better times in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These photographs were taken in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The next exhibit, Mr President, is a map which is an enlargement of Exhibit 180. Mr Dubuisson, would that be Exhibit 242?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: A 50 per cent chance of being right. Again, Mr President, if we could ask this not be put on the ELMO, simply because it identifies the location of Witness X's residence. Witness X, taking a look at the map before you and you see your house marked number 1, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: That whole area that is inside the circle or inside this rectangle, that is your mahala, that is your neighbourhood, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: What was the approximate ethnic split in that neighbourhood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think about 90 per cent Muslim, 90 or 95 per cent. I could probably put a list together, because there were about seven Croatian homes which were fully occupied.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: So seven Croatian homes and the balance of them belonged to Muslims, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: We will get back to that exhibit in one moment. I wanted to ask you a few questions about the activities that took place after May 1992 and you said that there were more and more HVO soldiers in the Busovaca area after May 1992, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you ever speak to any of your Croat neighbours regarding the pressure that was put on the Croats to join the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I had a friend with whom I worked at the Vatrostalna factory. For many years we worked together, some time in 1992, and I cannot recall all of this, but it was five or six years ago, let us say in September or October this friend came to me and said whether I could help him with some food supplies, the companies were no longer working, he had no money, he did not want to put on the HVO uniform, he did not want to -- that he spent his savings, that he had no food supplies and that he needed some in order to stay there. I told him that I had some because I knew him from before, and there was never any quarrel between us. I gave him some food supplies which is what he was asking for. Later I heard, not officially, that he was later forced to put on the HVO uniform and that he was killed in 1994; I believe it was 1994, maybe 1993, but in any event he was killed. It may have been from a shell from the mortar that they were using, so it could have been an accident.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On another occasion I asked a different friend, I had known him a long time, why he went to church now, whereas before he never went and we had talked about it before because (redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were other things, this is just sketching things out, so that I would present a picture that there were some pressures in Busovaca, this was five or six years ago. I may have not said everything as it happened chronologically and I may not have remembered everything in this moment, so if asked additional questions I may remember more.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Witness X, did your first neighbour who came to you for help and you gave him food, did he tell you what would happen if he did not join the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean what could have happened to him if he did not join? I did not speak about that in any detail with him, nor did I ask him any detailed questions, but whoever wanted or did not want, you know that all these companies collapsed and all the media were under the HVO control, and those who did not want to join the HVO, who did not have additional means -- people were running out of means, because those in the HVO were supplied regularly, they would get all the food and everything else that was needed, because this was kind of a pressure, I do not know how else to call it, so the people in a way had to go and join.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Witness X, was this taking place at the same time that the Serbs were leaving the area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. At first that is not how it went. There was not as much pressure, people mostly left voluntarily. I could not explain this. Those who felt that -- those who were able-bodied and those who were ardently Croatian, and then as days and months go by, you could notice more weapons, more uniforms, weapons were being carried all over, home and elsewhere. No one would part with their weapons, so that was a form of pressure for the Muslims to move out. I remember on 22nd or 23rd about 100 or 200 metres away from our neighbourhood, in another street, they provoked a young man whose name was Mirsad Delija. They called him out from his house and they shot him dead there. I thought that that was a clear sign of intimidation, they wanted the Muslims to leave at any price. I heard people say this would be Herceg-Bosna, so whoever likes that, fine. I even heard from these Croats who thought that they were not saying much, but actually they were, that whoever takes control of something that he -- that whatever territory the Croats take, it will stay Croatian, that whatever the Serbs do it will be Serbian and we were the victims from whom this was to be taken. Both sides thought like that, even though we lived there for centuries, together with the others. That is how I understood it, because there was no one else to take it away from except Muslims, because later on, they had a truck that they paraded around the neighbourhood on which an anti-aircraft gun was mounted, so they would come to the neighbourhood four or five times during a week. All these were forms of intimidation. On one occasion, I think this person was even under age, 15 or 16 years old, the road that goes through my neighbourhood, this soldier had a uniform on, I saw that he was a child, he was 15 or 16, he started shooting from his rifle and two men came to me and they told me, "why are you shooting?". I said, "I was not shooting, I have no weapons to shoot from", and he said, "it was not me, it was you, you have a rifle". I said, "I saw very well who shot", but I could not prove it. It was impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Witness X, let me talk to you about the Serbs leaving the area and one of the Serbs told you that your turn would come. Did any of the Serbs tell you how much money they were paying to be taken from the area and who they were paying the money to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I believe I said something about the Serb insist my statement, maybe not enough. In the Vatrostalna company, there were Serbs and Croats and Muslims who were all employees there. I think that there were equal numbers of Muslims and Croats, but there were fewer Serbs, maybe there were only a total of 2 per cent in the area. I had good relations both with Croats and Serbs, the ethnic group and religion was not a matter for me, as long as I could talk to people. So I had friends who were Serbs and Croats. So I asked one, whose name was Vojo Mujkic, he was from Podjele, he was a Serb from the Busovaca area, I asked him, "why are you leaving?"; he said that they were not leaving because they wanted to leave, they had to leave and after they left, it would be our turn, the turn of the Muslims. Then I saw them selling some of their belongings in the marketplace, they could not take them along or something, it was too much for them. I told them, "why are you selling it?". He said, "we cannot transport all this". I said, "where are you going? There is HVO in Kiseljak? You want to go to Zenica? You cannot go there. Where are you going to go?" Then he said, "they organised it, Kordic organised a collection centre in Podjele for Serbs from Travnik, Vitez, Zenica, wherever else. The price is about 1,000 German marks if you go on your own, that is without any belongings, but if you have a car then the price is higher, 2,000, maybe 3,000, depending on what you are transporting with you", so those who had a car would pay for that, those who did not own a car would go in buses, and they would go to Kobiljaca where the frontlines between the army and the Serbs were and that is where they were turned over and I do not know where they went from there.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Witness X, was there a time when you were walking past Dario Kordic's house in Busovaca where you saw some HVO soldiers that you knew outside the house and did you ask them what they were doing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I forgot to mention it. Some time starting in May 1992, there were barricades around Busovaca which were getting bigger and bigger. There was one outside of Busovaca, I do not know if I can see it here on the map, then there was another one near Kordic's house which I passed by there regularly on the way to the town, where there were people standing sitting around, five or six men, soldiers I mean, guarding the house and I knew them. I asked one of them who had worked with me in the company, "what are you doing here? What are you guarding here? Are you guarding Kordic?". He said, "no, we are not guarding Kordic, we are guarding Herceg-Bosna". I said, "oh, Herceg-Bosna", and he said, "yes, it is Herceg-Bosna we are guarding". I moved on towards my house. So the main Tisovacka street is there and then there was a crossroad and there was a checkpoint there and from thereon, my neighbourhood begins. There were two HVO soldiers there and one stopped him. I knew him and he knew me, because I would pass his house all the time and he asked me where I was going and I said I was going home. He said, "what home?" , and I said, "my own home". He said, "do you have ID?" I said, "please do not pretend you do not know me, you are my neighbour". He said, "I do not know anyone, just give me the papers". I gave him the IDs, he did not need them because he knew me. Then he said, "okay, this time it is fine, you may go". Then there was this other checkpoint maybe 300 or 400 metres further up the road, past our neighbourhood towards Tisovac and so on --

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Going back to these individuals in front of Kordic's house, did you ask them at that time what it meant to be protecting Herceg-Bosna and if so, what did they say in response?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not ask -- I do not remember.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. Let us move on to the conflict itself. You said that the conflict in Busovaca started on 25th January 1993, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: After that, did you see an HVO anti-aircraft weapon near your mahala that was shooting on to Muslim houses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, above our mahala, our neighbourhood, there is high ground and there is wood behind it and then there is some open fields, mostly Croats live there, so there was a wood over there, not very big, and there were some anti-aircraft machine-guns and guns and maybe a few mortars.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Just turning back to this exhibit, is that point 4 on the photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was not just one, there were several over here, but at point number 4, there was an anti-aircraft machine-gun placed.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me move ahead to when the soldiers came and took the men out of your mahala, out of your village. Did you see these soldiers, and were they HVO soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I saw soldiers, obviously they were all HVO soldiers. For the most part they had masks on, that is some kind of a stocking with openings for eyes, so I could not recognise them. There was an older man there, maybe around 60 and another one, men whom I met over a period of time, the young man, but the other ones I could not recognise because they wore masks.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: So you did recognise two of the soldiers that came?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Were they from Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, from Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: After that, were the rest of the Muslim residents and the Muslim refugees driven out of the rest of their homes in your mahala?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When the arrests took place, all the Muslim men who had stayed were arrested and everybody from the refugees except for women, children and elderly men, they left them, but the rest of them were taken away. After that, all this abuse, mistreatment started regarding the refugees from Jajce, so some left under the auspices of the Red Cross, some found a way out that way and there was also a Croat who was helping people move out so that the whole thing happened very quickly, so these refugees from Jajce all left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Have you got many questions, Mr Kehoe, because please try and get down to the essentials. I wanted to -- can you end with your questions before the break, please? Is it possible or not? Because the witness made a very long statement, with very many details and I think that the judges could very clearly see what the witness had been through. Maybe you have two or three things to make more precise and point out? I am simply going back to your summary now. Could you ask a couple of very precise questions, because if not we will have to make the break now and then end with your examination-in-chief before the cross-examination, so have you many things you want to point out now?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I do not have many things, Mr President. I do not think I can do it in two or three questions, candidly. I leave it to you, Mr President, whether you take the break now or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I am thinking here of the interpreters. Everybody has started to feel tired and also the witness himself is probably tired because of his long statement. I asked you before that because I thought you had only a couple of points you wanted to raise. If you wanted to do another direct examination from the start, that was another matter, so I think we are all tired, the judges including. We are going to make a break now and we will resume in 15 minutes. (4.15 pm) (A short break) (4.40 pm)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please have the accused brought in. We will resume now. (Accused brought in)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr Kehoe, according to your summary, what are the points that you would like to point out with Witness X?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: At this juncture, Mr President, the point we would bring out is that with regard to his particular neighbourhood, that first HVO moved into houses that belonged to the Muslims, one of which was Zoran Marinic, another was Mirko Milic. Those two houses are reflected in numbers 2 and 3 in the chart. Thereafter, Croats moved into the area from other areas with the authority or with licences or permits by the HVO authorities. It comes up, of course, because a question was raised even just this morning about whether or not the people that went in there were all refugees. The fact of the matter is HVO soldiers from Busovaca like Zoran Marinic took over a Muslim residence. The other feature --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The witness said that there were people that moved in those houses, so the witness does not need to repeat that, because I even jotted that down. The witness has simply to speak about those facts which he did not mention during his statement. If not, we will at some stage have to put an end to it and have the cross-examination start, because I have the responsibility for it. Please ask the questions which will very precisely give complementary moments to complete the statement, but the statement has been very complete and I would like to commend the witness for that, so please do it very quickly and after that, we will go on to cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr President, I just will focus on those particular points. Witness X, after the Muslims either left or were driven out of your mahala, did members of the HVO come in and take over some of the houses in your mahala?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the people, mostly people from Busovaca, also from village Ravne, moved into those privately-owned weekend houses and also into the houses of the Muslims who used to live there permanently. I said that in some houses they would stay for two or three days --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, that was already said. Please proceed to another question, Mr Kehoe now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Witness X, were two of the houses that they moved into on this particular map that is before you, Exhibit 240, did Zoran Marinic move into the house marked with number 2 and Mirko Milic, did he move into house marked with number 3?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this was the house, the weekend house of a man from Zenica and number 3 is the house of the brother of (redacted) who used to live in Germany at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: You knew, because you saw Zoran Marinic, that he was a member of the HVO military police, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I would see him every day, because the distance was some 50 to 100 metres from the house where he used to live, he moved into somebody else's house, from that house to my house. It can be seen on the map.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you see him wear a military police patch on his uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I would see him, he mostly wore the patch of military police.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: You said that there were searches at your house on 23rd April 1993. Those searches were not done -- were done by other members of the HVO and not Zoran Marinic and Mirko Milic, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, those were other people, not Zoran nor Mirko Milic.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me move ahead to the actual burning of your house and the killing of your neighbours. One of your Croat neighbours called the police that night, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: And the next morning, you went to the police station to give a statement, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Was that the civilian police or the military police that you went to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was the civilian police. There were two policemen that came by car, I know their names, Slavko Katava and Ivica Vidovic. They came and said that I had to give a statement, but the best thing would be for me to go to the police station. I went into the car and drove down there and I met some people I knew there, as I used to live in the neighbourhood, so I went into the office and I asked them to take me out of the area and as I said --

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Witness X, let me ask you a question. Did you tell the civilian police that Zoran Marinic had been responsible for the killing and burning in your mahala the night before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they asked me who did it and I said, "you know much better who did it than I, probably", because he was probably asked to do so, otherwise I do not think somebody would come on his own just in there to kill somebody. I did not really know Zoran too much when he used to go to school, I would sometimes give him a cigarette if he asked it from me. We went out from the police and they asked me and my wife to go into that house where we spent the night and I asked whether Zoran Marinic had been arrested because he committed a crime and he said, "yes, he was arrested" and my wife said that she could see him when she was going back from Kacuni where she went to reach for UNPROFOR and she went and UNPROFOR was in Hotel Kiseljak, but she cross him when she was going in one direction and he in the other direction around Kacuni, but I simply gave her a sign to remain silent, because regardless of the fact whether he was arrested or not, there is law and if somebody commits a crime, that person has to be arrested, but no, he was not arrested. Even last year he was seen going around Busovaca as a free man.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Excuse me, Witness X, here we are not at the case against Zoran Marinic. I think that is very important. What the Prosecutor would like to know is whether he belonged to the HVO and this is linked to the chain of command, but this is the trial of General Blaskic and not of Zoran Marinic. Please proceed, Mr Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: To conclude on this point, Witness X, Zoran Marinic was a member of the military police and to your knowledge he was never prosecuted or arrested for the crimes that took place in your mahala on the evening of 26th April 1993, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, never a single person who committed a crime was arrested there, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr President, at this time we would offer into evidence under seal Exhibits 240, which is the map that is before us, and also the series of photographs which also have some family members belonging to Witness X. If I might have one moment to consult with my colleagues, Mr President, I believe that I have completed. Thank you, Mr President, I have no further questions. Thank you, Witness X.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr Prosecutor. Mr Nobilo is going to ask questions. This is a very usual thing, this is a trial of General Blaskic and now the Defence is going to ask questions. Mr Nobilo, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Good evening, Mr X.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good evening.

utterances.speaker: MR NOBILO
utterances.text: Did the police when you arrived at the police station to give the statement linked to those killings, did the police tell you that they needed to know your address?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They did not tell me, they asked me whether there was a weekend house in my neighbourhood where I could live.

utterances.speaker: MR NOBILO
utterances.text: Did the police, once you went out of the police station, did they know where you were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I mentioned in my statement here, I decided I did not want to go into any of the weekend houses up there, because they already came to kill me in my house, it would be even worse in a weekend house. They asked me whether I had a --

utterances.speaker: MR NOBILO
utterances.text: Excuse me, could you please shortly answer --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, if there could be some break between the question and the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I interrupted the witness on purpose. We heard your story. Could you please answer whether in the police station after you left it they knew where you were going to stay for the following days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they took me to a certain place which they chose, to a person who I did not know and that person did not know me. After that, I went back to the centre of the town, thinking they would be looking for me again and that is what happened. I was in the centre in a street where there were lots of Muslims and nobody knew where I was, nobody could know exactly where I was, they were looking for me for seven days, I have got proof of that, people told me about it.

utterances.speaker: MR NOBILO
utterances.text: Out of what you have just said, can I conclude that in the police station, once you left the police station, that they did not know any more where you lived?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They did not know, but I was not at the place where they brought me to.

utterances.speaker: MR NOBILO
utterances.text: After you were hiding at those places you left Busovaca. You did not have contact with the police, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct. I said that only my wife on 24th May went to the police station to ask for a permit to leave Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR NOBILO
utterances.text: Were you a member of the BH-Army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR NOBILO
utterances.text: You gave a statement to the investigators of the Office of the Prosecutor, this is the only statement which is not dated, and in the first paragraph, you say that you are a member of the army of BiH --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I should correct you, there are two statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: One statement is a summary and one is a proper statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Is that one or two statements?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I have two, Mr President, I am just correcting counsel. Two were sent to counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr Hayman? This is something that we would be able to clarify, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: We have a Serbo-Croatian statement with a half page English summary and we have an English language statement, that is what our records reflect we have. Only one English language statement which is the witness's actual statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Okay, so this is an incident. There was a problem of terminology. You are both right. There are two documents but maybe not two statements in these proceedings, so please, Mr Nobilo, use both documents. I think this incident is now behind us, and Mr Kehoe, I gave you 50 per cent credit for it. There are two documents that you gave to the Defence. Mr Nobilo, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. We are going to clarify things very quickly. At the beginning of this statement you gave you said at the moment that you gave the statement you are a member of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and that you have been its member since 16th April 1992, I believe.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me clarify this. It says that I was a member of the army since 16th April, but I never was in that army, not before the conflict but yes, after the conflict, in 1993 when I went out, when I managed to get out, I joined the army. I think that you can understand me. I have suffered so much, so it was logical for me to join them. Now I am not a member of the army. On 20th December 1994 I was demobilised.

utterances.speaker: MR NOBILO
utterances.text: According to a military document, did you join the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina on 16th April 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I joined the Bosnian army on 31st May when I joined it at Kacuni. You cannot be a member of the army if you are not in it actually between 1992 and 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR NOBILO
utterances.text: What is in your military papers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It says that I am a member of the army as of 31st May 1992, and actually when I joined it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr Kehoe, do you have an objection you wanted to raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr Nobilo?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So is that statement correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The statement that I belonged to the army between 31st May 1993 and 20th December 1995, that is correct, then I was demobilised.

utterances.speaker: MR NOBILO
utterances.text: So to the investigators of the Office of the Prosecutor, you did not tell the truth when you said --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: At this point I object. The man said he was a member of the army from 31st May 1993 until 20th December 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Your Honour, if you please, I would like to find out whether this was a mistake, wrongly written down, or the witness gave the wrong statement to the investigators of the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right, now I am turning myself to the witness. This is an important question for the Defence. Witness X, please be calm, Defence counsel is asking a legitimate question of you and they would like to know whether you were a member of the army or not and in your statement, you said that you were the member of the army. You said that for you, there is a difference between enrolling and participating in the operations. I am not quite agreeable with you, you are either a member of something or not. There is no trap in that question, especially not coming from a judge, that is the parties neither ask questions that would be a trap, so please could you say that when you gave the statement you said you were the member of the Bosnian army. Could you please say whether at that time you were officially a member of it, yes please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the HVO police that I said that I belonged to the HVO? That is something I deny. They were themselves witnesses that I was not a member.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Excuse me, the fact to participate in the operation is not really the question. We want to know whether you were, even only in theory, a member of the Bosnian army. Mr Nobilo, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that on 31st May 1993 up until 20th December 1995 I was a member of the Bosnian army. I think that was clear enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did you say to the investigators of the Office of the Prosecutor that you were a member of the army since 16th April 1992; did you tell it to them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot recall, I gave statements twice at Zenica. Maybe the interpreter did not interpret that correctly, there must have been a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, let us proceed. During direct examination you said that just before the conflict in January, around 21st January 1993, two or three days before that, a large number of Muslim civilians had left Busovaca. Do I remember that well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, on 21st January.

utterances.speaker: MR NOBILO
utterances.text: What I ask you now is why did those civilians leave before the conflict broke out? How did they know there would be a conflict?

utterances.speaker: MR NOBILO
utterances.text: (redacted). This friend said it to another friend and so rumours spread. You know when people start to have fear then you believe many things.

utterances.speaker: MR NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. During direct examination, you said that the conflict or the war in April 1993 started on April 14th. How do you know that? How did you remember that it was 14th April? What happened on that date so that you concluded that the war broke out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As you can see on this map, here is where I lived, in this part, in this area (indicates), and after our neighbourhood, where you can see the woods and meadows, so there are the woods and they were the HVO frontlines and the army frontlines and I was down hill and so you could hear large detonations and shootings and I could see some Croats. I had a feeling they were some 500 metres away from Busovaca and that there were shootings and they were also the Croatian refugees who had moved in, they were also preparing to go out, because they thought the army would go into Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR NOBILO
utterances.text: So according to you, the war started on 14th April 1993, because you saw it yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It started on 25th May, when the conflict broke out.

utterances.speaker: MR NOBILO
utterances.text: But yes, the actual war in April started on the 14th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not actually at that place, but I could hear the detonations and I concluded there was conflict going on and I know because when they took us from the police to that house where we spent the night, the night before the tragedy, my wife told a policeman, "kill us here now and do not take us anywhere else". He swore at her and gave her her rifle and said, "you can shoot at me and kill me because I had been injured from the people from the army". I said, "it is not my fault, I did not tell anybody to go there and fight".

utterances.speaker: MR NOBILO
utterances.text: You said that the Croats were forced in various ways to join the HVO, so I ask you now, can we say that most Croats that were capable to take arms did wear a uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, mostly those people who were of military age did wear military, even some elderly people, some pensioners.

utterances.speaker: MR NOBILO
utterances.text: How old were the youngest and the oldest people in uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a 15 or 16 year old boy whom I saw shoot in my neighbourhood and I could see he was underage, but all the others were of age.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could not see whether that was civilian or military police, because it was 10.00 or 11.00 in the night when they arrived, but they investigated the case probably that night, they did not allow UNPROFOR to come, but they did not allow them and they said that they would settle everything and there was no need for UNPROFOR to come.

utterances.speaker: MR NOBILO
utterances.text: When you were at the police station, were you expressly forbidden -- not given permission to leave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, twice.

utterances.speaker: MR NOBILO
utterances.text: Did you ask to be put in Kaonik rather than leave because you would be safer there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not tell them to put me in Kaonik, because I knew what was going on there. I just wanted to be in prison here because it was safer there in the town.

utterances.speaker: MR NOBILO
utterances.text: You described the exchanges that took place and you said that everybody needed to find a family in Zenica and then organise the exchange in that way. Let me ask you this: was this a voluntary exchange of families and people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was voluntary, but the Muslims who had remained in -- stayed in Busovaca wanted to leave at any cost and the members of the HVO in Zenica, they also insisted to have their families move over. I think that there was talk about ethnic cleansing both ways, so that all the Croats would be moved from Zenica over here and then all the Croats from Zenica, and all the Muslims from Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR NOBILO
utterances.text: So that was the kind of exchange?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In a Croatian house.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I object to the line of questioning on this score, it is a protected witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr President, many Muslims live in Croatian houses and vice versa. It is something that this witness can identify.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I do not object to the specific question, I do object with a protected witness when a counsel comments on where a protected witness is living.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr President, with your permission, I only ask about the type of house, not who the owner is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Is it really essential for you, Mr Nobilo? Is it really very important?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: It was already stated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr Hayman? This is not a very good answer, Mr Hayman, it is not because the answer was given that the objection has not got its weight, but maybe in the transcript, we could put some kind of an embargo to this answer?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Doubtless we can do that, a redaction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr Hayman, we are going to redact. So in the transcript, this answer will not appear.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: As to the geographic place, Mr President? I would hope, "in a Croatian house", can remain in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I will ask, it was a question about the owner I think, as far as the village or the town, it is maybe less important. Mr Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: My issue, Mr President, was counsel highlighting the specific town where a protected witness is living. That was my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I suggest that we delete in the transcript the name of the village. The Trial Chamber has got its responsibility towards the protection of witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: One more question: have you ever seen our client Tihomir Blaskic in Busovaca at any time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I never saw him in person, I saw him on television.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr President, thank you very much, this concludes our cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Would you like to reply now, Mr Kehoe?

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Just briefly. You were asked some questions on cross-examination about if you told the police on the morning after your house was put on fire, if you told the police where you were going to be residing. During that conversation, did the police tell you that Zoran Marinic had been arrested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did not tell them where I would live, I did not know where I would live, but they took me in a car to a place, to a house where they told me to stay with my family, and regarding the arrest of Zoran Marinic, yes they confirmed that he was arrested, but since my wife interjected and denied it, they looked at one another and then I nudged her and told her to be silent, because this was murder, and you can imagine the tragedy that I went through, that I had my house burned down and my family was there with me. I may have omitted something, you lose your concentration when you recall the images of things that happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Any other questions, Mr Kehoe?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No, Mr President, thank you very much. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge Riad?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness X. I will just ask you a few questions, I do not need a long answer, but some precision. In your very lengthy testimony, you mentioned that anti-aircraft was shooting on Muslim houses; do you remember that, that anti-aircraft was shooting at Muslim houses? Could this anti-aircraft belong to somebody else than the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was no possibility for it to belong to anyone else, because we did not possess any weapons. Everything was under the HVO control, all the communications lines were under the HVO control, so we could not move anything there. I actually even saw the emplacement where it was, and I knew the soldiers who were there. At that time, there was no reason for it not to be seen, they had placed it there very early on.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: It was an army operation, it was an HVO army operation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: The houses which were being shot at, did they have any military importance, or were they just civilians' houses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that on 26th January when the Muslims saw what was going on, when they were being put together then taken to Kaonik, they offered some resistance, there were about ten rifles there, about 20 people, there were some hunting rifles, some Karabins, maybe a few pistols and maybe some hand grenades that were purchased from Croatian friends or something, so when this conflict broke out, that was about a couple of hours really, the HVO had superior power. That is from this position number 4, there was some shooting. It was 500 to 1,000 metres. From that position you could see clearly every single house. These houses were all civilian houses, there was nothing military about them.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: No depot of ammunitions or fighters hiding in those houses or that sort of thing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, just locals, no depots.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: You said the shooting came from 1,000 metres away, it was not so far? Where did the shooting come from, exactly? Do you have an idea?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This shooting came from point number 4, there was a wood there, maybe it was 5 to 6 to 10 metres high emplacement and there was positions there. It is about 100 metres away from my house and they were shooting across over to the other side, maybe up to 1,000 metres away.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: You mentioned that people were taken to dig trenches in the frontlines. What happened to these people, do you know anything which happened to them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not sure, they were taken there, I can confirm that, I know a man, a Muslim, he was organising these men and he is still alive to date. I talked to him a little bit and then after the war, I talked more, some people protected them, some people beat them. I heard that two or three of them were killed from our own army, because when you shoot you do not know who is who.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: You also mentioned that among other things the Muslims who remained and who did not leave were arrested by the military police. Was there any special reason for arresting them? Were they caught fighting? Why were they arrested, since they wanted to stay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were not captured during the fighting, they did not have weapons, those were my neighbours who lived there. There were no weapons there, there were no uniforms there. They were simply able-bodied. That is how it happened. There was this collection centre or camp in Kaonik where they were taken.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: So they were arrested because nobody wanted them to stay, is that the reason?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably that is -- I believe that was the reason. This was a Muslim settlement, further on there was a Croatian settlement called Ravan. I remember one occasion in 1992 when I worked, I was building an auxiliary building, property, and a Croat came by and he asked me why was I building this. I said, "well I needed a garage here for my car" and he said, "are you not leaving here?", and I said, "no, where should I go, leave my own house?", and then he said, "very well". I think my view was that Busovaca was to be cleansed because Croats considered it to be Croatian. On one occasion I heard there was a celebration of the anniversary of the independence of Croatia, and a politician, a Croatian politician said that this would be Croatia and that in the future, Busovaca would be called Croatian Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: In short, the Muslims were expelled as part of the cleansing of Busovaca; is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, 100 per cent I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Judge Shahabuddeen, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Witness, I have the impression that you told Defence counsel, Mr Nobilo, that you yourself never saw Colonel Blaskic in person, you only saw him on television, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Do you see Colonel Blaskic in court today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Can you point to him, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Indicates).

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Is that the same gentleman whom you saw on television?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: How often did you see him on television, roughly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Listen, this was local Busovaca television, and they were taping things and then broadcast it later. I did not pay too much attention to either watch or listen to him, because I had not known him from before and I did not have particular interest in following his statements. I did know Kordic personally, we had worked together.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you see Kordic on TV?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
