utterances.text: Did you ever see Colonel Blaskic in company with Mr Kordic on TV?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that this was local television and so they were showing just the persons who were speaking and so they were not showing group shots.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Then I thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I will be very brief. Witness X, you said when speaking about Croats who were members of the HVO that there were people who were enlisted by force. Please answer briefly to my very simple question. In the HVO, were there some kind of mercenaries, the HVOs, people who were paid for it; for example, some people that told you, "yes, I have to go to church now because now I wear an HVO uniform", or were these people deeply devoted to the cause or were they a mixture of both? Were simply part of them just mercenaries who enlisted because they thought they could have some profit from it, or were there people who were extremely devoted to it with deep convictions? Could you tell us, because you lived through it all.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You could talk about two kinds of soldiers here. I did not say that some rough force was used, the force was more material, because he did not have means of survival, he had no food and things like that, so those who did not join were not getting these things. As far as the mercenaries are concerned, as far as I know, all HVO members received salaries, whereas we did not. I have a friend who is a Croat who currently lives in Zenica. He used to live in Busovaca, and I learned from him they had a supplement of 50 marks assistance of sorts. Also the locals and the refugees here in Busovaca received this. Then he told me that he would either have to give up -- he was faced with a choice that he would have to give up either this supplement of 50 marks or the Bosnian pension to which he was entitled. He had to make that choice and he did, he opted for the pension.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: In your opinion, these financial aids that helped people, that they were better paid than the Bosnian soldiers; where did that money come from? Was the HVO wealthy? Did it come from Croatia or from some kind of political tax that had been levied? I would like to simply know your opinion.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My personal opinion is that the HVO itself did not have such financial resources which would -- these would be very large sums of money. What I read in the papers was that Tudjman, that is Croatia, financed this army in Herceg-Bosna, I do not know how else to describe it, so that they would be paid, because we in the army had no salaries towards the end of the war, we would get about 40 marks a month so that we could buy cigarettes, whereas they were receiving 400 to 500 marks.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: I am going to ask you a question that might seem paradoxic to you, and I am sorry in advance in case I shock you, but in troubled times, there are many variations in mentality and here is my question: you told us that there were Croats that maybe did not take you in their house, but did help you, help you in one way or the other, you used to have good relations with them before the war, and good understanding. My question is: are there amongst Muslims people for various reasons, because they wanted profit or because of mixed marriages or convictions, that joined the HVO? I do not ask you in general whether there were people in Busovaca, because you know that region?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not in Busovaca. After the conflict at Kaonik regarding the JNA barracks, a representative of the HVO, I do not know his name, but I knew him from -- in fact two of them came to our neighbourhood, we gathered there, the Muslims, so that they could give us this information, so he said, "we came here to invite you to join the HVO voluntarily, because this is your Busovaca". Then we kind of looked at each other and kept silent, then we said, "why should we all go to the HVO, why do we not all join the army if we are fighting the JNA and the Serb Army under the same flag, then we will be all together there". Then he said that flag did not mean anything to them, that had nothing to do with them. Then I said, "how come it means nothing? Stjepan Kljujic is in the government, he was legally elected". He said, "we broke all relations with him, we have no contact with him, we do not want to". I said I was not going to go to the HVO, because I am not even a member of the army, but I would like us all to go under the same flag, whether it be the HVO or the flag of Bosnia. If we were going to fight against the JNA, we should all do it together. I could not think of a conflict between Croats and Muslims, because traditionally we lived together and we would for instance work together if somebody was building a house, things like that. I could not even imagine to any fight with the Serbs, our neighbours, here in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I never thought there were Croats in Bosnia, I thought they were Catholics. If he was born here, he would be a Bosnian and not a Croat, same with the others, if he were born in Croatia, he would be a Croat, but I was wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness X. The end of the statement. I think that you had the opportunity to say everything that you want the. This Trial Chamber would like to thank you for your coming here. Please remain seated because you are a protected witness and we have to ensure your protection. We are now at the end of a long day and the interpreters had to translate many difficult things, so I suggest that we adjourn for today and we will start again tomorrow morning. (5.30 pm)
